title: What are @NamedQuery and @NamedNativeQuery in JPA? How do they differ from an inline @Query, and why are they validated at startup?
keyPoints: @NamedQuery defines a reusable JPQL query with a name, declared on the entity, and validated at application startup
@NamedNativeQuery is the same idea for raw SQL, but SQL syntax is not validated at startup by the JPA provider
Startup validation means a broken JPQL query fails fast at boot, not at runtime when a user hits the path
Naming convention is EntityName.queryName, such as Account.findByStatus
Inline @Query on a Spring Data repository method is also validated at startup for JPQL, but is local and not reusable by name
Named queries can be overridden in orm.xml without recompiling, useful for tuning in production
@SqlResultSetMapping maps native query results to entities or DTOs when column names do not match

s1_definition.oneliner: @NamedQuery defines a reusable, startup-validated JPQL query on an entity; @NamedNativeQuery does the same for raw SQL; both are pre-compiled and fail fast if the query is broken.
s1_definition.profdef:
JPA provides two annotations for declaring named, reusable queries directly on entity classes.

- **@NamedQuery** – declares a JPQL query with a unique name on an entity class; the JPA provider parses and validates it at application startup, caching the parsed query for reuse.
- **@NamedNativeQuery** – declares a native SQL query with a unique name; it is registered at startup but the SQL syntax is not validated because the provider does not parse vendor-specific SQL.
- **Startup validation** – the process where the JPA provider checks all JPQL named queries when the EntityManagerFactory is built, ensuring field names, entity names, and parameter usage are correct before any user request arrives.
- **@SqlResultSetMapping** – maps the columns returned by a native query to entity fields or DTO constructor parameters when the column names do not match automatically.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a named query is like a pre-approved standard form kept in the bank's forms cabinet. Compliance checked every form once when it was added, so every teller who pulls it knows it is valid and just fills in the blanks for the parameters. An inline query is like a teller writing a request freehand at their desk each time -- convenient and local, but the standard named form is the official, reusable, pre-validated one. Validating at startup is compliance checking every form in the cabinet the moment the branch opens, so a broken form is caught before any customer is served.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Application Startup:

  EntityManagerFactory builds
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Parse all @NamedQuery (JPQL)       │
  │  ├── Validate entity names          │
  │  ├── Validate field names           │
  │  ├── Validate parameter bindings    │
  │  └── Cache parsed query             │
  │                                     │
  │  Register all @NamedNativeQuery     │
  │  └── SQL is NOT validated           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
       │
       ├── All JPQL valid? → Application starts
       └── Any JPQL broken? → Application FAILS TO START
```

```text
  Named Query Lifecycle:

  @NamedQuery on Entity
       │
       │ startup: parse + validate + cache
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  Cached Parsed Query │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │
    ┌────────┴────────┐
    ▼                 ▼
  EntityManager     Spring Data
  .createNamedQuery  Repository method
  ("Account.find")   findByStatus()
    │                 │
    ▼                 ▼
  Set parameters    Auto-matched by
  Execute           EntityName.methodName
```

```text
  @NamedQuery vs @Query vs Derived:

  ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ @NamedQuery          │  On entity → reusable, validated
  ├─────────────────────┤
  │ @Query               │  On method → local, validated (JPQL)
  ├─────────────────────┤
  │ Derived query        │  findByStatus → auto-generated
  └─────────────────────┘
  Priority: @NamedQuery > @Query > Derived
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A @NamedQuery defines a reusable JPQL query with a name, declared on the entity class, and the JPA provider parses and validates it once at application startup. If the JPQL has a typo, references a field that does not exist, or misuses a parameter, the application fails to start with a clear error instead of shipping a broken query that only explodes at runtime when a user hits that path. A @NamedNativeQuery is the same idea for raw SQL, but the SQL is not validated at startup because the provider does not parse vendor-specific SQL.

The difference from an inline @Query on a Spring Data repository method is mostly about location and reuse. A named query is declared centrally on the entity and can be invoked by name from multiple repositories and from the EntityManager directly. An inline @Query keeps the text right next to the method, which is more discoverable, but it is local and not reusable elsewhere by name. Spring Data also validates inline JPQL at startup, so the fail-fast benefit applies to both, but named queries are the JPA standard and offer orm.xml override for production tuning.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj declares core business queries as named queries on the entity because they are reused across multiple services. He keeps one-off queries as inline @Query for discoverability. The named queries can be overridden in orm.xml without recompiling, which proved valuable when the DBA optimized a slow query in production without a code release.

Remember one sentence: @NamedQuery is a reusable, startup-validated JPQL query declared on the entity; @NamedNativeQuery is the same for SQL but without startup validation.
